payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the image into pencil drawing
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Are the scene's major surfaces represented with pencil-like surface marks or graphite texture?
node.criteria: Pass if pencil-like surface mark-making is visibly established across major surfaces through fine directional strokes, hatching, form-following marks or convincing deposited graphite texture. Inspect the marks themselves: they must read as drawing material on the depicted surfaces, rather than merely random noise superimposed on photographic texture. Fine strokes and retained color do not disqualify pencil drawing. Fail if substantial surfaces show only photographic material texture, desaturation or undifferentiated grain without convincing pencil-like marks. This condition concerns surface mark-making, not whether the underlying tonal gradients and reflections have also been converted to pencil shading. Use unknown only when the visible evidence cannot establish the character or extent of the marks.
node.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the instruction to change the image into pencil drawing. Inspect surface marks across the carrots, sprouts, potato slices, plate, table and glassware, using the source to distinguish newly drawn texture from original material texture. Evaluate the direction, articulation and distribution of the marks, not color reduction or contour strength. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation.

The visible speckling does not form convincing directional strokes, hatching, or form-following graphite marks across the major surfaces.

The edited image is desaturated and grainy, but the carrots, sprouts, potato slices, plate, table, and glassware largely retain smooth photographic shading and material texture. There are no clearly articulated directional strokes, hatching, or convincing deposited graphite marks across the major surfaces; the visible grain reads as an overlay rather than pencil mark-making.

The edited image shows fine, directional, form-following graphite-like strokes and mottled deposited texture across the food, plate, tablecloth, and glassware. These marks visibly alter the surfaces from the source’s photographic textures and read as pencil drawing rather than merely desaturation or uniform grain.

The edited image shows fine, directional graphite-like strokes and deposited texture across the food, plate, tablecloth, and glassware. The marks follow surface forms and shading rather than appearing as undifferentiated noise; the source’s photographic textures are visibly rendered with a drawn quality.

d1_shading_modeling: The binding already targets the right distinction, and the repeated traces consistently identify real negative evidence: desaturation, grain, and softened edges are present, while much of the pitcher, glass, food, plate, and table still reads as photographic tonal modeling. Do not weaken the criterion or treat those surface marks as sufficient. The reference label “partial” is an aggregate constraint, not proof that this specific shading check should pass: this node can correctly fail while other requested changes account for partial progress. Preserve that separation when deciding the node outcome. For better robustness, make the binding explicitly ask for an independent pass/fail/unknown judgment of this tonal-rendering criterion, based on whether graphite-like value modeling broadly replaces photographic gradients and reflections across the scene; distinguish that from unrelated progress such as desaturation or texture. Use unknown only for genuinely insufficient visual evidence, not low confidence or disagreement with the aggregate. Traces are valid, queried, and dependency-free, so there is no transport or schema issue to repair.
